questions.q: The transfer of heat from the hotter part of an object to its colder part is called:
o: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
Evaporation
questions.a: Conduction. The chapter defines conduction as the process of heat transfer from the hotter part of an object to the colder part.

questions.q: One end of an iron rod is kept in a flame. Which statement correctly describes how heat travels along the rod?
o: Each particle that gets heated passes the heat to its neighbour, but stays in its own position
The hot particles travel from the heated end to the cold end, carrying the heat with them
Heat jumps from the flame straight to the far end without passing through the rod
Cold particles from the far end move towards the flame to collect heat
questions.a: Each heated particle passes the heat on to its neighbour, and so on, but the particles themselves do not move from their positions. This is conduction.

questions.q: (a) What is conduction? (b) In which state of matter does heat transfer take place mainly by conduction?
s: (a) Conduction: the transfer of heat from the hotter part of an object to its colder part, the particles passing heat to their neighbours without moving
(b) Solids
questions.a: (a) Conduction is the process of heat transfer from the hotter part of an object to the colder part; each heated particle passes the heat to its neighbour without leaving its position. (b) In solids, heat is transferred mainly by conduction.

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'When a steel spoon is left in hot dal, the particles of the spoon move from the hot end up to the handle and carry the heat with them.'
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the spoon is heated by conduction, in which each particle passes heat to its neighbour but the particles do not move from their positions
questions.a: False. The spoon gets heated by conduction: each heated particle passes the heat on to its neighbouring particle, but the particles themselves stay in their positions.

questions.q: In a science class in Indore, students take an aluminium strip about 15 cm long and fix four pins on it with wax, about 2 cm apart. They label the pins I, II, III and IV, with pin I nearest the free end. The strip is clamped to a stand and the free end is heated with a spirit lamp. Pin I drops first, then pin II, then pin III, and pin IV drops last. (a) Which pin is nearest the flame? (b) Why does each pin drop? (c) Why do the pins not all drop together? (d) Name the process of heat transfer shown here.
s: (a) Pin I
(b) Heat reaches the wax holding the pin and melts it
(c) Heat travels along the strip from the hot end to the colder end, so it reaches the nearer pins first
(d) Conduction
questions.a: (a) Pin I, at the heated end. (b) When heat travelling along the strip reaches a pin, the wax holding it melts and the pin falls. (c) The heat moves gradually along the strip from the hot end towards the colder end, so it reaches pin I first, then II, III and IV. (d) Conduction.

questions.q: Assertion (A): When one end of a long iron rod is kept in a fire, its other end becomes hot only after some time, not at once. Reason (R): In conduction, heat passes from each particle to its neighbouring particle along the rod. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: heat is passed on from particle to neighbouring particle step by step along the rod, so it takes time to reach the far end.

questions.q: Consider these statements about conduction. I. Conduction needs a medium whose particles pass on the heat. II. In conduction, the heated particles leave their places and carry heat to the colder part. III. In conduction, heat moves from the hotter part of an object to its colder part. Which of these statements are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and III only. Conduction needs a medium and heat flows from hotter to colder parts, but the particles do not move from their positions, so statement II is wrong.

questions.q: Rehana bends a copper strip into an L shape and heats it at the bend. Three pins are fixed with equal amounts of wax, measured along the strip from the bend: pin P is 2 cm along the longer arm, pin Q is 8 cm along the longer arm, and pin R is 5 cm along the shorter arm. (a) Which pin falls first? (b) Which pin falls last? (c) Give the reason for this order.
s: (a) Pin P, the one 2 cm from the heated bend
(b) Pin Q, the one 8 cm from the heated bend
(c) Heat spreads by conduction from the heated bend along both arms and reaches nearer pins first, so the order is P, R, Q
questions.a: (a) Pin P (2 cm from the bend). (b) Pin Q (8 cm from the bend). (c) Heat travels by conduction from the heated bend along both arms of the strip, and reaches the nearer wax first. So the pins fall in order of their distance along the strip from the heated point: P (2 cm), then R (5 cm), then Q (8 cm).

questions.q: Gita rests one end of a steel ruler and one end of a wooden ruler of the same size on a hot tawa, with a small blob of butter on the far end of each ruler. After 3 minutes the butter on the steel ruler has melted, but the butter on the wooden ruler has not. (a) How did heat reach the butter on the steel ruler? Say what the particles of the ruler do. (b) Why did the butter on the wooden ruler stay solid?
s: (a) By conduction: each heated particle of the steel passes the heat on to its neighbour, from the hot end to the colder end, while the particles stay in their positions
(b) Wood is a poor conductor (insulator) of heat, so heat does not pass through it easily and too little reached the butter to melt it
questions.a: (a) By conduction. The end on the tawa gets hot; each heated particle of steel passes the heat to the next particle, and so on along the ruler to the butter, but the particles themselves do not move from their positions. Steel is a good conductor, so this happens quickly. (b) Wood is a poor conductor (insulator): it does not let heat pass through it easily, so not enough heat reached the far end to melt the butter.

questions.q: A jaggery (gur) maker in Muzaffarnagar needs a new pan for boiling cane juice. For the heat to spread well across the base, a wax pin fixed 12 cm from the heated end of a strip of the pan's metal must fall within 2 minutes. He tests strips of the same size over the same flame. Time for the pin to fall: copper 45 s, aluminium 60 s, brass 110 s, iron 180 s. Price of a pan: copper Rs 9000, aluminium Rs 5000, brass Rs 7000, iron Rs 3000. (a) Arrange the four metals from the best to the poorest conductor of heat, using the data. (b) Which metals meet the 2-minute limit? (c) Which pan should he buy if he wants to spend as little as possible? Justify with the data. (d) What material should the pan's handles be made of, and why? (e) His son says, 'Copper conducted heat best, so it is the only sensible buy.' Judge this claim.
s: (a) Copper, aluminium, brass, iron (the faster the pin falls, the better the conductor)
(b) Copper (45 s), aluminium (60 s) and brass (110 s); iron (180 s) takes longer than 120 s
(c) Aluminium: it meets the limit and is the cheapest of the three metals that do (Rs 5000 against Rs 7000 and Rs 9000); iron is cheaper but fails the limit
(d) Wood (a poor conductor), so heat does not pass easily to the hand
(e) Not justified: copper is the fastest, but aluminium already meets the 2-minute need for Rs 4000 less, so the extra speed is not needed
questions.a: (a) Copper, aluminium, brass, iron: heat travelled the 12 cm fastest in copper and slowest in iron. (b) Copper, aluminium and brass; iron took 180 s, more than 2 minutes (120 s). (c) Aluminium. Of the three metals that pass, it costs the least (Rs 5000, against Rs 7000 for brass and Rs 9000 for copper). Iron is the cheapest pan, but it fails the 2-minute limit. (d) Wood, a poor conductor of heat, so heat from the hot pan does not pass easily to his hands. (e) The claim goes too far. Copper is the best conductor in the test, but aluminium also meets the need (60 s, under 120 s) and costs Rs 9000 - Rs 5000 = Rs 4000 less, so copper is not the only sensible buy.

questions.q: Which of these materials is a poor conductor (insulator) of heat?
o: Porcelain
Steel
Aluminium
Iron
questions.a: Porcelain. The chapter lists glass, wood, clay and porcelain as poor conductors of heat; steel, aluminium and iron are metals, which are good conductors.

questions.q: Woollen clothes keep us warm in winter mainly because:
o: air trapped in the pores of the wool is a poor conductor and reduces heat flow from the body to the surroundings
wool produces heat of its own and passes it to the body
wool is a good conductor and brings heat from the surroundings to the body
wool reflects the cold away from the body
questions.a: Woollen fabric traps air in its pores; air is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the flow of heat from our body to the surroundings and we feel warm.

questions.q: Match each item in Column I with the reason in Column II. Column I: 1. Cooking pans made of metal; 2. Tea served in clay or porcelain cups; 3. Two thin blankets instead of one thick blanket; 4. Outer walls of hollow bricks. Column II: (p) the air between the layers acts as an insulator; (q) a good conductor lets heat pass quickly to the food; (r) trapped air keeps the house warm in winter and cool in summer; (s) a poor conductor keeps the tea hot for longer.
questions.a: 1-q, 2-s, 3-p, 4-r: metal pans conduct heat well to the food; clay and porcelain are poor conductors that keep tea hot; air between two thin blankets acts as an insulator; air trapped in hollow bricks keeps houses warm in winter and cool in summer.

questions.q: (a) Why are cooking utensils generally made of metals? (b) Why does tea kept in a clay cup stay hot longer than tea kept in a steel tumbler?
s: (a) Metals are good conductors of heat, so heat passes easily from the flame to the food
(b) Clay is a poor conductor (insulator), so heat does not pass out of the tea easily
questions.a: (a) Metals are good conductors of heat, so heat passes easily from the flame to the food being cooked. (b) Clay is a poor conductor of heat, so it does not let heat pass out of the tea easily, while steel, a metal, lets it escape faster.

questions.q: Here are six things found in a home: an aluminium pressure cooker, a wooden rolling pin, a porcelain cup, an iron tawa, a woollen shawl and a glass bowl. (a) List the ones made of good conductors of heat. (b) List the ones made of poor conductors of heat. (c) Give one use from the list that depends on a good conductor and say why. (d) Give one use from the list that depends on a poor conductor and say why.
s: (a) Good conductors: the aluminium pressure cooker and the iron tawa
(b) Poor conductors: the wooden rolling pin, the porcelain cup, the woollen shawl and the glass bowl
(c) A use of a good conductor, such as the iron tawa letting heat pass quickly from the flame to the roti
(d) A use of a poor conductor, such as the woollen shawl trapping air that reduces heat loss from the body, or the porcelain cup keeping tea hot
questions.a: (a) Good conductors: aluminium pressure cooker, iron tawa (both metals). (b) Poor conductors: wooden rolling pin, porcelain cup, woollen shawl, glass bowl. (c) The iron tawa is used for cooking because iron, a metal, lets heat pass quickly from the flame to the roti. (d) The woollen shawl keeps us warm because wool traps air, a poor conductor, which reduces heat flow from the body (or: the porcelain cup keeps tea hot longer).

questions.q: Assertion (A): Houses whose outer walls are made of hollow bricks stay comparatively cool in summer. Reason (R): The air trapped in hollow bricks is a good conductor of heat. Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Hollow bricks keep houses cool in summer and warm in winter because the trapped air is a POOR conductor of heat, not a good one.

questions.q: On a cold morning Ravi wears one thick cotton jacket. His sister wears a thin vest, a thin shirt and a thin sweater, which together are as thick as Ravi's jacket. Who is likely to feel warmer? Give two reasons based on the chapter.
s: His sister is likely to feel warmer
Air is trapped between her layers of clothing
Air is a poor conductor of heat, so these layers reduce heat flow from her body to the cold surroundings, just as two thin blankets keep us warmer than one thick one
questions.a: His sister. Air gets trapped between her thin layers of clothing, and air is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the heat flowing from her body to the cold air. This is the same reason two thin blankets keep us warmer than one thick blanket.

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'A steel mug lined on the inside with a thick layer of porcelain will keep coffee hot for a shorter time than a plain steel mug of the same size.'
s: Verdict: False
Reason: porcelain is a poor conductor (insulator), so the lining slows the heat passing out of the coffee into the steel, and the coffee stays hot longer, not shorter
questions.a: False. Porcelain is a poor conductor of heat, like clay, which is why coffee in porcelain cups stays hot longer. The porcelain lining slows the flow of heat from the coffee to the steel and out to the surroundings, so the lined mug keeps the coffee hot for a LONGER time.

questions.q: A tiffin maker in Lucknow tests three lunch boxes of the same size, each filled at 8 am with hot rice at 70 degrees Celsius. Box X is a plain steel box (Rs 150). Box Y is the same steel box kept inside a cloth bag (Rs 250). Box Z is a double-walled steel box with a sealed layer of air between its walls (Rs 600). Rice readings at 9 am: X 52, Y 57, Z 63; at 10 am: X 38, Y 44, Z 55 degrees Celsius. Riya eats lunch at 9 am and Sonu at 10 am; each wants the rice at 40 degrees Celsius or more, and wants to spend as little as possible. (a) By how many degrees did the rice cool in each box from 8 am to 10 am? (b) Why did box Z keep the rice warmest? (c) Which box should Riya buy? Justify with the data. (d) Which box should Sonu buy? Justify with the data.
s: (a) X cooled by 32, Y by 26 and Z by 15 degrees Celsius
(b) The sealed air between the walls is a poor conductor, so it slows the heat flowing out of the rice
(c) Box X: at 9 am its rice is still at 52, above 40, and it is the cheapest
(d) Box Y: at 10 am box X has fallen to 38, below 40, while Y is at 44; Y costs less than Z, so it is enough
questions.a: (a) X: 70 - 38 = 32; Y: 70 - 44 = 26; Z: 70 - 55 = 15 degrees Celsius. (b) Steel is a good conductor, but the layer of air between Z's walls is a poor conductor, so heat leaves the rice much more slowly. (c) Riya: box X. At 9 am its rice is at 52 degrees, already above 40, so the costlier boxes give her nothing she needs. (d) Sonu: box Y. By 10 am box X is down to 38, below 40, but box Y is at 44; Y meets the need for Rs 250, so the Rs 600 box Z is not needed.

questions.q: The warden of a hostel in Shimla must choose winter bedding. He wraps three identical bottles of water at 60 degrees Celsius in a cold room: P in one thick woollen blanket (2 kg, Rs 900 per bed), Q in two thin woollen blankets laid one over the other (1 kg each, Rs 1000 per bed), and R in one thin woollen blanket (1 kg, Rs 500 per bed). After 6 hours the readings are P 33, Q 39 and R 24 degrees Celsius. He wants bedding that keeps a bottle at 35 degrees Celsius or more after 6 hours, at the lowest cost. (a) By how many degrees did each bottle cool? (b) Which bedding should he buy? Justify with the data. (c) P and Q have the same weight of wool. Explain why Q kept its bottle warmer. (d) Why did R do worst? (e) A shopkeeper says, 'The heaviest single blanket is always the warmest choice.' Evaluate this claim using the data.
s: (a) P cooled by 27, Q by 21 and R by 36 degrees Celsius
(b) Q: it is the only one at 35 or more (39); P (33) and R (24) fail, so Q is worth the extra Rs 100 over P
(c) Air is trapped between the two thin blankets; air is a poor conductor, so it reduces the flow of heat out of the bottle
(d) One thin blanket has less wool and less trapped air, so heat flows out of the bottle most easily
(e) Not correct: P and Q weigh the same, yet Q kept the bottle 6 degrees warmer (39 against 33), because of the layer of air between its blankets
questions.a: (a) P: 60 - 33 = 27; Q: 60 - 39 = 21; R: 60 - 24 = 36 degrees Celsius. (b) Q, two thin blankets. Only Q keeps the bottle at 35 degrees or more (39); P falls to 33 and R to 24, so although P is Rs 100 cheaper it does not meet the need. (c) Woollen fabric traps air, and between two thin blankets there is also a layer of trapped air. Air is a poor conductor of heat, so it reduces the heat flowing out; that is why two thin blankets are preferred over one thick blanket. (d) R is a single thin blanket with the least wool and trapped air, so heat passes out of the bottle most easily and it cooled the most. (e) The claim is wrong. P and Q have the same weight of wool, but Q kept the bottle 39 - 33 = 6 degrees warmer, because the air trapped between its two blankets is a poor conductor. The arrangement matters, not only the weight.

questions.q: The transfer of heat by the actual movement of particles of liquids and gases from one place to another is called:
o: Convection
Conduction
Radiation
Infiltration
questions.a: Convection. In convection, heat is carried by the actual movement of particles of liquids and gases.

questions.q: In Activity 7.2, the paper cup hanging above the burning candle rises. This happens because the air in the cup:
o: warms up, expands, becomes lighter and rises
cools down, contracts and becomes heavier
is pushed upward by the candle's light
loses all its particles to the flame
questions.a: The air around the flame heats up; as the air in the cup warms, it expands, occupies more space, becomes lighter and rises, lifting the cup.

questions.q: (a) In which two states of matter is heat mainly transferred by convection? (b) Give one example of convection from the chapter.
s: (a) Liquids and gases
(b) One example, such as water in a beaker heated from below, or smoke or warm air rising above a flame
questions.a: (a) Liquids and gases. (b) For example, water in a beaker heated at the centre of its base gets heated throughout by convection (or: warm air above a candle rises and lifts a paper cup; smoke rises because it is warmer than the air around it).

questions.q: A grain of potassium permanganate is placed at the centre of the base of a beaker of water, and a candle is kept right below that point. The coloured streak:
o: goes up in the middle and comes down along the sides
goes down in the middle and up along the sides
stays at the bottom and never moves
spreads only sideways along the base
questions.a: It goes up in the middle and comes down along the sides: the water heated at the centre of the base expands, becomes lighter and rises, while cooler, heavier water from the sides comes down to take its place.

questions.q: Nirmala heats a pan of water on a stove to make tea. Only the base of the pan touches the flame. (a) Which water in the pan gets heated first? (b) What happens to this water once it is heated? (c) What does the cooler water near the sides do? (d) Until when does this movement go on? (e) Name the process by which the whole pan of water gets heated.
s: (a) The water at the bottom of the pan
(b) It expands, becomes lighter and rises
(c) The cooler, heavier water comes down to take its place and then gets heated in turn
(d) Until the entire volume of water gets heated
(e) Convection
questions.a: (a) The water at the bottom, nearest the flame. (b) It expands, becomes lighter and rises. (c) The cooler, heavier water from the sides comes down to take its place, gets heated and rises in turn. (d) This cycle continues until the entire volume of water gets heated. (e) Convection, heating by the actual movement of water particles.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a beaker heated from below, heat reaches the water at the top mainly by convection. Reason (R): In convection, the particles stay in their positions and pass the heat on to their neighbours. Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. Water is heated mainly by convection, but in convection the particles actually move from one place to another; staying in position and passing heat on describes conduction.

questions.q: At a festival, a paper lantern that is closed at the top and open at the bottom has a small flame fixed at its open end. After a short time the lantern rises into the air. (a) What happens to the air inside the lantern? (b) Why does the lantern rise? (c) Which activity in the chapter shows the same idea?
s: (a) The air inside is heated by the flame and expands, occupying more space
(b) The warm air becomes lighter than the cooler air around it and rises, carrying the light paper lantern up
(c) Activity 7.2, in which the paper cup above the burning candle rises
questions.a: (a) The flame heats the air inside the lantern; it expands and occupies more space. (b) The heated air becomes lighter than the surrounding cooler air, so it rises and carries the light paper lantern with it. (c) Activity 7.2: the inverted paper cup hung above a burning candle rises for the same reason.

questions.q: Consider these statements. I. Air expands and becomes lighter when it is heated. II. Convection, like conduction, needs a medium. III. In convection, the heated part of a liquid sinks to the bottom. Which of these statements are correct?
o: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and II only. Heated air expands and becomes lighter, and convection needs a medium whose particles move. Statement III is wrong: heated liquid becomes lighter and RISES; the cooler, heavier liquid comes down.

questions.q: A student builds a closed box with two short chimneys, A and B, on its top. A burning candle is placed inside the box right under chimney A. When a smoking incense stick is held just above chimney B, the smoke goes DOWN into chimney B and then comes out of chimney A. (a) What happens to the air above the candle? (b) Why is air drawn into the box through chimney B? (c) Explain the path of the smoke. (d) Name the process and give one example of it in nature from the chapter.
s: (a) The air above the candle is heated, expands, becomes lighter and rises out through chimney A
(b) Cooler, heavier air from outside comes in through chimney B to take the place of the rising air
(c) The smoke is carried along with this moving air: down chimney B, across the box and up and out with the hot air through chimney A
(d) Convection; land and sea breezes are an example in nature
questions.a: (a) The candle heats the air above it; this air expands, becomes lighter and rises out through chimney A. (b) Cooler, heavier air outside moves in through chimney B to take the place of the rising air. (c) The smoke is light and is simply carried by the moving air: down chimney B, across the box and up chimney A with the heated air, so its downward movement at B shows the air current. (d) Convection, heat transfer by the actual movement of air; land and sea breezes are convection in nature.

questions.q: In Activity 7.2, which change would make the cup above the candle rise LESS?
o: Using a smaller candle flame in the same place
Using a bigger candle flame in the same place
Moving the same candle closer below the cup
Placing a second candle below the same cup
questions.a: Using a smaller candle flame in the same place: the air in the cup gets heated less, so it expands less, becomes less light, and lifts the cup less. Each of the other changes heats the air in the cup more.

questions.q: The movement of cooler air from the sea towards the land during the day is called:
o: Sea breeze
Land breeze
Radiation
Infiltration
questions.a: Sea breeze: during the day the land heats faster, warm air over it rises, and cooler air moves from the sea to the land.

questions.q: In Activity 7.4, identical bowls of soil and water are kept in sunlight for 20 minutes. Which result is observed?
o: The temperature of the soil rises more than that of the water
The temperature of the water rises more than that of the soil
Both rise by exactly the same amount
The temperature of the soil falls
questions.a: The soil's temperature rises more than the water's, showing that soil heats up faster than water.

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'On a seashore at night, the air above the sea is warmer than the air above the land.'
s: Verdict: True
Reason: at night the land cools down faster than the sea water, so the air above the sea stays warmer and rises
questions.a: True. In the absence of sunlight the land cools faster than the water in the sea, so the air above the sea is warmer; it rises and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea (land breeze).

questions.q: Answer briefly about a coastal area. (a) Which gets heated faster in sunlight, land or water? (b) In which direction does the breeze blow during the day? (c) In which direction does the breeze blow at night?
s: (a) Land
(b) From the sea towards the land (sea breeze)
(c) From the land towards the sea (land breeze)
questions.a: (a) Land heats up faster than water. (b) By day, cooler air moves from the sea to the land: the sea breeze. (c) At night, cooler air moves from the land to the sea: the land breeze.

questions.q: Windows of houses in coastal areas are usually placed facing the sea so that:
o: the cool sea breeze can come in during the hot day
the warm land breeze can come in during the day
heat radiated by the sea warms the rooms at noon
rainwater from the sea can enter the house
questions.a: The cool sea breeze, which blows from the sea to the land during the day, can come in and relieve people from the heat.

questions.q: Match Column I with Column II for a seashore. Column I: 1. Soil in sunlight; 2. Sea water in sunlight; 3. Air above the land at noon; 4. Cool air at midnight. Column II: (p) heats up and cools down slowly; (q) moves from the land towards the sea; (r) heats up and cools down fast; (s) gets warm and rises.
questions.a: 1-r, 2-p, 3-s, 4-q: soil heats and cools fast, sea water slowly; at noon the air above the warmer land gets warm and rises; at midnight cooler air moves from the land towards the sea (land breeze).

questions.q: Fishermen at a jetty in Puri record the air temperature 1 m above the beach sand and 1 m above the water at the far end of the jetty, and watch which way the smoke from their cooking fire on the beach drifts. At 1 pm the air over the sand is at 36 degrees Celsius and the air over the water at 30 degrees Celsius, and the smoke drifts inland. At 2 am the air over the sand is at 21 degrees Celsius and over the water at 26 degrees Celsius, and the smoke drifts out to sea. (a) At 1 pm, which air is warmer and by how many degrees? (b) Name the breeze blowing at 1 pm. (c) Explain why the smoke drifts the other way at 2 am. (d) By how much did the air over the sand and over the water each cool from 1 pm to 2 am, and what does this show?
s: (a) The air over the sand, by 6 degrees Celsius
(b) Sea breeze
(c) By 2 am the land has cooled below the sea, so the warmer air above the sea rises and cooler air moves from the land to the sea (land breeze), carrying the smoke out to sea
(d) Over the sand it cooled by 15, over the water by only 4 degrees Celsius: land cools much faster than water
questions.a: (a) The air over the sand: 36 - 30 = 6 degrees Celsius warmer. (b) Sea breeze: the warm air over the land rises and cooler air moves in from the sea, so the smoke drifts inland. (c) At 2 am the air over the land (21) is cooler than over the sea (26); the air above the sea is warmer and rises, and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea, a land breeze, so the smoke drifts out to sea. (d) Over the sand: 36 - 21 = 15 degrees; over the water: 30 - 26 = 4 degrees. Land cools much faster than water, just as it heats faster.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In coastal areas, a sea breeze blows during the day. Reason (R): At night, land cools down faster than the water in the sea. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The sea breeze blows by day because the land heats faster than the sea, so warm air over the land rises and cooler sea air moves in; R is true but explains the land breeze at night, not the sea breeze.

questions.q: A beach hotel in Kovalam plans (1) rooms with windows facing the sea, and (2) an open-air dinner area between the hotel kitchen and the sea, used from 8 pm to 11 pm. The kitchen chimney gives out a lot of smoke and is on the land side of the dinner area. (a) In which direction does the breeze blow at 9 pm? (b) Explain why it blows that way. (c) What will happen to the kitchen smoke during dinner? (d) Suggest a better position for the kitchen and give the reason. (e) Is plan (1) a good one? Justify.
s: (a) From the land towards the sea (land breeze)
(b) At night land cools faster than the sea, so the warmer air above the sea rises and cooler air from the land moves towards the sea
(c) The land breeze carries the smoke from the kitchen towards the sea, straight over the diners
(d) Place the kitchen on the sea side of the dinner area (or away from the line between land and sea), so the night breeze carries the smoke out to sea, away from diners
(e) Yes: by day the cool sea breeze blows from the sea to the land, so sea-facing windows let it in and relieve the heat
questions.a: (a) From the land towards the sea, a land breeze. (b) After sunset the land cools faster than the sea water, so the air above the sea is warmer and rises, and cooler air moves from the land to the sea. (c) The kitchen is on the land side, so the land breeze will blow its smoke over the dinner area towards the sea, right onto the diners. (d) Put the kitchen on the sea side of the dinner area (or well to one side), so the night breeze carries the smoke out over the sea, away from the guests. (e) Yes. During the day the land heats faster, and the cool sea breeze blows from the sea to the land; windows facing the sea let it in, as the chapter says coastal houses do.

questions.q: On a hot, sunny afternoon, campers on the shore of a very large lake feel a steady cool breeze. Which statement best explains it?
o: It blows from the lake to the land, because the land heats faster and the warm air above it rises
It blows from the land to the lake, because the hot land pushes its air outward
It blows from the lake to the land, because the water heats faster and its air sinks
There can be no such breeze, because it happens only beside a sea
questions.a: It blows from the lake to the land: like the sea, a large water body heats more slowly than land, so the warm air over the land rises and cooler air moves in from over the water, just as in a sea breeze.

questions.q: The heat of the Sun reaches the Earth by:
o: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
Infiltration
questions.a: Radiation. The chapter says the heat of the Sun reaches us through radiation, which needs no medium.

questions.q: Which mode of heat transfer does NOT need a material medium?
o: Radiation
Conduction
Convection
Both conduction and convection
questions.a: Radiation. Conduction and convection need a medium whose particles help transfer heat; radiation needs no material medium.

questions.q: (a) Which colour of clothes is more comfortable to wear in summer? (b) Give the reason.
s: (a) White or light-coloured clothes
(b) They reflect most of the heat that falls on them
questions.a: (a) White or light-coloured clothes. (b) Light-coloured clothes reflect most of the heat that falls on them, so we feel more comfortable in them in summer.

questions.q: Water is being heated in a steel pan on a gas stove, and Arjun, standing near it, feels warm. (a) How does heat pass from the flame to the pan? (b) How does all the water in the pan get heated? (c) How does the warmth reach Arjun's face? (d) Which of these three processes needs no medium? (e) Name the traditional Himalayan heater in which all three processes take place when it is used for cooking and warming a room.
s: (a) Conduction
(b) Convection
(c) Radiation
(d) Radiation
(e) The bukhari
questions.a: (a) By conduction, from the flame to the utensil. (b) By convection, through the movement of water particles in the pan. (c) By radiation from the flame and the hot pan. (d) Radiation needs no material medium; conduction and convection do. (e) The bukhari, an iron stove burning wood or charcoal, used in the upper Himalayas.

questions.q: A hot kadhai is taken off the flame and hung on a hook on the wall, away from the stove. It cools after some time mainly because:
o: it radiates heat to its surroundings
cold air flows into the metal of the kadhai
it absorbs heat from the room
its particles move out into the air
questions.a: All objects radiate heat; a hot utensil kept away from the flame cools down by radiating heat to its surroundings.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Conduction and convection cannot take place where there is no material medium. Reason (R): In both conduction and convection, particles of matter help to transfer the heat. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: in conduction particles pass heat to neighbours and in convection particles move, so both need a medium of particles; only radiation needs none.

questions.q: A potter in Khurja takes a freshly fired clay pot out of the kiln and hangs it by a rope from a beam in a shed where the air is still. (a) The pot touches only the rope, yet it cools down. By which process does it mainly lose heat? (b) His helper says, 'If there were no air around the pot, it would not cool at all.' Is he right? Give a reason. (c) A second hot pot of the same kind is set down on an iron sheet instead. Which pot will cool faster, and why?
s: (a) Radiation: all objects radiate heat, and the hot pot radiates heat to its surroundings
(b) No: radiation needs no material medium, so the pot would still lose heat by radiation without air; only conduction and convection need a medium
(c) The pot on the iron sheet: besides radiating, it also loses heat by conduction into the iron, a good conductor that it touches
questions.a: (a) Radiation. All objects radiate heat; a hot object kept away from the fire cools by radiating heat to its surroundings. (b) He is not right. Conduction and convection need a medium, but radiation does not, so the pot would still lose heat by radiation even with no air around it. (c) The pot on the iron sheet cools faster. It radiates heat like the hanging pot, and in addition heat passes from it into the iron sheet by conduction, because iron is a good conductor and the two are in contact.

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'An electric iron (press), switched off and stood on its wooden stand away from any flame, cannot cool down, because wood is a poor conductor and nothing else touches it.'
s: Verdict: False
Reason: all objects radiate heat; the hot iron loses heat to its surroundings by radiation, which needs no contact or medium, just as a hot utensil kept away from the flame cools down
questions.a: False. All objects radiate heat. The hot iron gives out heat to its surroundings by radiation, which does not need contact or a material medium, so it cools down even on a wooden stand, just as a hot utensil kept away from the flame cools after some time.

questions.q: In a hot desert town, a family wants the water in its rooftop tank to stay as cool as possible in summer. Which colour should they paint the tank?
o: White, because light colours reflect most of the heat falling on them
Black, because dark colours reflect the most heat
Black, because dark colours absorb heat and then lose it at once
Any colour, because colour does not affect heat from the Sun
questions.a: White: light-coloured surfaces reflect most of the heat that falls on them, while dark surfaces absorb more heat.

questions.q: On a cold, clear winter morning in Leh, a trekking club pitches two identical small tents side by side in bright sunshine at 9 am. One tent is made of dark brown cloth and the other of white cloth. A thermometer hangs inside each. Both read 4 degrees Celsius at the start, and the air outside stays cold. At noon the dark tent reads 21 degrees Celsius and the white tent 12 degrees Celsius. (a) By how many degrees did each tent warm up? (b) Which tent took in more of the Sun's heat, and why? (c) How did the Sun's heat reach the tents when the air around was cold? (d) A member concludes, 'White clothes are the best choice in every season.' Judge this using the data.
s: (a) Dark tent by 17, white tent by 8 degrees Celsius
(b) The dark tent, because dark surfaces absorb more heat while light ones reflect most of it
(c) By radiation, which travels directly from the Sun and needs no medium
(d) Not correct: in the cold the dark tent gained far more heat (17 against 8 degrees), so dark clothes are more comfortable in winter; white suits summer
questions.a: (a) Dark tent: 21 - 4 = 17 degrees; white tent: 12 - 4 = 8 degrees Celsius. (b) The dark tent: dark surfaces absorb more heat, while light surfaces reflect most of the heat falling on them. (c) By radiation, which brings the Sun's heat directly and needs no medium, so the cold air did not stop it. (d) The conclusion is wrong. The data show a dark surface takes in far more of the Sun's heat (17 degrees against 8), which is welcome in the cold, so dark clothes are more comfortable in winter and light clothes in summer.

questions.q: The process by which water evaporates from trees and plants is called:
o: Transpiration
Condensation
Precipitation
Infiltration
questions.a: Transpiration: water also evaporates from trees and plants through transpiration.

questions.q: In Activity 7.5, the same amount of water is poured through bottles of clay, sand and gravel. Through which does the water seep fastest?
o: Gravel, because the spaces between its particles are the widest
Clay, because its particles are the smallest
Sand, because it is the lightest
All three at the same speed
questions.a: Gravel: the spaces between gravel particles are wider than those in sand and clay, so water seeps through it most easily.

questions.q: (a) What is infiltration? (b) What are aquifers?
s: (a) Infiltration: the process of surface water seeping through soil and rocks
(b) Aquifers: underground layers of sediments and rocks that store water in their pore spaces
questions.a: (a) Infiltration is the process of surface water seeping through soil and rocks. (b) Aquifers are the underground layers of sediments and rocks that store water in their pore spaces.

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'Clouds form when water vapour rises, cools down and condenses.'
s: Verdict: True
Reason: water vapour from evaporation and transpiration rises, cools and condenses into clouds, which then bring rain, snow or hail
questions.a: True. Water vapour rising from oceans, rivers, lakes and plants cools down high up and condenses to form clouds; the clouds bring rain, snow and hail (precipitation).

questions.q: In a growing town near Jaipur, many families now pump water from bore wells, and the open grounds have been covered with concrete. The panchayat notices that the water level in the old wells is going down every year. An engineer explains that rainwater must seep into the ground and be stored in the underground layers of sediments and rocks before wells can use it. She suggests rainwater harvesting and recharge pits. (a) Name the process by which rainwater seeps into the ground. (b) What are the underground water-storing layers called? (c) Give one reason from the passage why the groundwater is falling. (d) Name one way suggested to replenish it.
s: (a) Infiltration
(b) Aquifers
(c) Too much water pumped from bore wells, or concrete limiting infiltration
(d) Rainwater harvesting or recharge pits
questions.a: (a) Infiltration. (b) Aquifers. (c) Excessive extraction through bore wells (or: concrete surfaces limit infiltration of rainwater). (d) Rainwater harvesting or recharge pits, which help replenish groundwater.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Covering more and more ground in a city with concrete can lead to falling groundwater levels. Reason (R): Concrete surfaces limit the infiltration of rainwater into the ground. Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: concrete stops rainwater from seeping in, so less water reaches the aquifers to replace what is drawn out.

questions.q: Wet clothes on a line dry faster on a sunny day than on a cloudy day. (a) Name the process by which the water leaves the clothes. (b) What is the Sun's role in it? (c) Where may this water end up next as part of the water cycle?
s: (a) Evaporation
(b) Heat from the Sun makes the evaporation of water faster
(c) The water vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds and can come down again as rain, snow or hail
questions.a: (a) Evaporation. (b) The heat from the Sun makes water evaporate faster, so clothes dry quicker on a sunny day. (c) The water vapour rises into the air, cools and condenses to form clouds, and returns to the Earth as precipitation (rain, snow or hail), flowing into water bodies or seeping into the ground.

questions.q: A team is looking for the best place to dig a new well. At which place is it most likely to find water easily?
o: Where the layers underground have wide, open and connected spaces between particles
Where there is a thick layer of solid rock with no openings
Where the ground is covered with a thick layer of tightly packed clay
Where the surface is covered with concrete
questions.a: Where the underground layers have wide, open and interconnected spaces: water infiltrates readily and is stored in such pore spaces (an aquifer), so a well there gets water easily.

questions.q: A village can afford one recharge pit to refill its falling wells. Site A is next to the panchayat office, 50 m from the roofs whose rainwater will be led into it; the ground there is clay. Site B is 400 m away near the school; the ground there is gravel, and the longer pipe costs Rs 30,000 more. In a test like Activity 7.5, 200 mL of water was poured through soil from each site: in 10 minutes 25 mL came through the Site A soil and 150 mL through the Site B soil. (a) How many times as much water came through the Site B soil as through the Site A soil? (b) Explain this difference using the chapter. (c) What is likely to happen to the rainwater led into a pit at Site A during heavy rain? (d) Which site should the village choose in spite of the extra cost? Justify with the data. (e) Explain how the chosen pit will help the wells, using the words infiltration and aquifer.
s: (b) The spaces between gravel particles are wider, open and connected, so water seeps through gravel much faster than through clay
(c) It seeps in very slowly, so the pit fills up and most of the water overflows or stands and runs off instead of reaching the groundwater
(d) Site B: its soil let 6 times as much water through, so far more of the rain reaches the ground; a cheaper pit that lets little water in does not solve the problem
(e) Rainwater in the pit seeps down through the gravel (infiltration) and is stored in the pore spaces of the aquifer, from which the wells draw water
questions.a: (a) 150 / 25 = 6 times as much. (b) Water seeps fastest through gravel and slowest through clay, because the spaces between gravel particles are wider, open and interconnected. (c) The clay lets water in very slowly, so in heavy rain the pit fills and most of the water overflows or runs off instead of seeping into the ground. (d) Site B. The test shows its ground lets 6 times as much water through, so the money spent there actually puts water back into the ground; the cheaper Site A pit would save Rs 30,000 but recharge very little. (e) Water led into the pit infiltrates through the gravel and is stored as groundwater in the pore spaces of the aquifer; the wells draw from this aquifer, so their level is replenished.

questions.q: A village in Kinnaur waters its fields from a stream fed by snowfields. The stream carries about 90 units of water a day in April and about 200 units a day in June, though very little rain falls in the valley in June. The fields need 120 units a day from April to June. In winter, when the fields need no water, the village can fill a storage tank from the stream: tank A holds 600 units and tank B holds 1000 units. (a) By how many units a day is April short of the need, and by how much does June exceed it? (b) Where does the extra water in June come from? (c) After a winter with very little snowfall, the village head says, 'The June flow will be the same, because the summer Sun shines just as strongly.' Judge this claim. (d) Which tank should the village build to cover April's shortfall (30 days)? Show your working.
s: (a) April is short by 120 - 90 = 30 units a day; June exceeds the need by 200 - 120 = 80 units a day
(b) In summer the Sun's radiation melts snow and ice on the mountains, and the water flows down into the stream
(c) Not justified: the snow that melts is replenished by fresh snow in winter; after little snowfall there is less snow to melt, so the June flow is likely to be lower
(d) Shortfall 30 x 30 = 900 units; tank A (600) is too small, tank B (1000) covers it
questions.a: (a) April: 120 - 90 = 30 units a day short. June: 200 - 120 = 80 units a day more than needed. (b) During summer some of the snow and ice on the mountains is converted to water by the Sun's radiation and flows down as the stream, so the flow rises even without much rain. (c) The claim is wrong. Strong sunshine can only melt the snow that is there; the melted ice is replenished by fresh snow during winter. After a winter with little snowfall there is less snow to melt, so the June flow will probably be lower. (d) April's shortfall is 30 units a day x 30 days = 900 units. Tank A holds only 600, which leaves 300 units short; tank B holds 1000, which covers the 900 units. The village should build tank B.

questions.q: Two identical towels each weigh 300 g when dry and 500 g when wet. At 9 am one is hung in a sunny courtyard and the other in a shaded verandah of the same house. At 1 pm the towel in the sun weighs 320 g and the one in the shade 420 g. (a) How much water has left each towel? (b) Why did the towel in the sun lose more water? (c) A neighbour says, 'Water evaporates only in sunshine.' Use the data to judge this claim.
s: (a) Sunny towel: 500 - 320 = 180 g; shaded towel: 500 - 420 = 80 g
(b) Heat from the Sun makes the evaporation of water faster
(c) Wrong: the shaded towel also lost 80 g of water by evaporation, only more slowly; the Sun speeds evaporation up, it is not needed for it
questions.a: (a) Sunny towel: 500 - 320 = 180 g of water; shaded towel: 500 - 420 = 80 g. (b) The heat from the Sun makes water evaporate faster, so the towel in the sun dried more in the same 4 hours. (c) The claim is wrong. The towel in the shade also lost 80 g of water, so evaporation went on without direct sunshine, only more slowly. The Sun's heat makes evaporation faster; it is not the only way water evaporates.
